title: Hospital operations monthly review
scenario: The hospital operations manager needs a concise review of activity for January–March 2026. They want to understand encounter volume, length of stay and 30-day readmission flags by department. A separate pharmacy lead wants a count of medication orders by therapeutic class and order status.
business_question: What do the supplied synthetic records show about activity, length of stay, recorded 30-day readmission flags and medication-order mix during the stated period?
data: assignments/data/synthetic_encounters.csv — 80 encounter records; one row per encounter.
assignments/data/synthetic_medication_orders.csv — 150 medication-order records; one row per order.
assignments/starter/healthcare_operations_assignment.xlsx — Excel workbook with raw data sheets and task instructions.
requirements: Keep the raw sheets unchanged; perform analysis in new sheets or PivotTables.
Calculate encounter count, mean length of stay, number flagged for 30-day readmission and the proportion flagged.
Summarise encounter count and mean length of stay by department.
Summarise medication-order counts by therapeutic class and order status.
Create one management-facing chart and a short written interpretation.
State the denominator, period, unit of analysis and at least three limitations.
steps: Open the starter workbook in Excel, LibreOffice Calc or ONLYOFFICE. Confirm both data sheets have the expected row counts.
Convert or retain each range as a structured table. Check date columns are dates and numeric columns are numeric.
Create a KPI area. Use COUNTA for encounter IDs, AVERAGE for length of stay, COUNTIF for readmission flags and divide flagged encounters by total eligible encounters.
Build a department summary using a PivotTable or equivalent SUM/COUNT/AVERAGE formulas.
Build a medication class by order status summary. Do not call orders administrations or dispensed medicines.
Choose a chart that answers a defined management question. Add a descriptive title, axis labels and reporting period.
Write a 150–250 word management note with findings, definitions, limitations and a recommended next validation step.

linux.tools: LibreOffice Calc or ONLYOFFICE; CSV import

windows.tools: Microsoft Excel, LibreOffice Calc or ONLYOFFICE

deliverables: Completed workbook with formulas/PivotTables and chart.
QA note listing row counts, date range, duplicate-key check and metric definitions.
acceptance: Encounter source has 80 records and unique encounter IDs.
Medication-order source has 150 records and unique order IDs.
Readmission proportion uses encounter-level denominator and is labelled as a recorded flag, not a causal outcome.
Order counts are labelled as orders, not administrations or dispensing events.
All reported totals reconcile to the supplied source data.
pitfalls: Do not average patient age or LOS across order rows after a one-to-many join; that would weight encounters by number of orders.
A 30-day readmission flag in a synthetic file is not a validated readmission measure.
Do not infer medication adherence, administration or clinical appropriateness from an order record.
portfolio: A polished workbook, short management note, metric dictionary and QA log. Remove any personal file paths and ensure only synthetic data are included.

title: SQL prescribing and encounter analysis
scenario: A pharmacy analytics team asks for a reproducible extract showing encounter volume by department and medication-order mix. They need class-level order counts and a cross-check of whether a join between encounters and orders changes the unit of analysis.
business_question: How many encounters occurred by department, and how are medication orders distributed by therapeutic class and order status?
requirements: Load both CSV files into SQLite using DBeaver or sqlite tooling.
Document table grain, primary key and foreign key relationship.
Write queries for row counts, distinct encounters, encounter count by department, order count by class and status, and encounters with at least one order.
Use a LEFT JOIN for encounter coverage and demonstrate how one-to-many joins affect row counts.
Use a CTE or subquery to aggregate orders before joining to encounter-level summaries.
Save executable SQL and a short findings note.
steps: Create a local SQLite database named healthcare_simulation.db.
Import each CSV as a table named encounters and medication_orders; preserve column names.
Run the starter script's schema checks and confirm key uniqueness.
Write each required query separately and compare count(*) with count(distinct encounter_id).
Build a CTE that aggregates medication orders per encounter before joining to the encounter table.
Save final SQL in your own solution file and export the result tables as CSV.

windows.tools: DBeaver Community or SQLite command-line tools

deliverables: SQL script with comments and named queries.
acceptance: Both source tables load with 80 and 150 records respectively.
Encounter IDs are unique in encounters and order IDs are unique in medication_orders.
A join result with multiple order rows is not described as encounter count.
Encounter coverage is calculated from distinct encounter IDs.
SQL outputs reconcile with Excel summaries from SIM-01.
pitfalls: A one-to-many join duplicates encounter attributes across order rows.
COUNT(*) after joining does not count unique encounters.
LEFT JOIN filters placed in WHERE may unintentionally convert the result into an inner join.
A medication order is not proof of administration, dispensing or adherence.
portfolio: Publish a README, commented SQL, result extracts generated from synthetic data, and a short explanation of join cardinality and validation.

title: Client request to final analytical handoff
scenario: A remote quality-improvement coordinator sends an incomplete request: 'Please analyse readmissions and medication patterns and send something useful by Friday.' You must clarify the scope, define the metrics, identify what the supplied data can support, produce a reproducible analysis and hand off findings professionally.
business_question: What can be responsibly answered from the supplied synthetic encounter and medication-order files, and what additional data or definitions are required before making a quality-improvement claim?
data: The synthetic encounter and medication-order CSV files from SIM-01 and SIM-02.
A blank request clarification template and handoff template in assignments/starter/.
requirements: Write five to eight clarification questions before analysis.
Create a concise analysis plan with population, period, unit of analysis, outcomes and exclusions.
Use Excel or SQL to create validated descriptive summaries.
Create a one-page dashboard or report with a metric dictionary.
Prepare an email-style handoff stating findings, limitations, unresolved questions and next steps.
Create a reproducibility README so another analyst can rerun the work.
steps: Clarify whether readmission means all-cause unplanned inpatient readmission within 30 days, which index discharges qualify, and how transfers/deaths are handled.
Ask whether medication patterns mean orders, administrations, dispensing or reconciliation records; the supplied data only contain orders.
Define the population and period; confirm whether all 80 encounters are eligible and whether follow-up is complete.
Write a data assessment: grain, keys, missingness, duplicates, date validity and data lineage.
Perform descriptive summaries and independently reconcile at least two key metrics.
Prepare a decision-oriented report; do not use causal language or claim medication effectiveness.
Draft a client handoff with what is known, what is not known, caveats, and an actionable request for additional data.
deliverables: Reproducible SQL or workbook and output extracts.
acceptance: The analysis explicitly separates encounters from medication orders.
Readmission definition and follow-up completeness are identified as unresolved unless supplied by the requester.
Medication orders are never described as administrations or adherence.
At least two key outputs are reconciled independently.
The handoff contains limitations, unresolved questions and next steps.
pitfalls: The brief is intentionally ambiguous; do not silently invent definitions.
The provided readmission flag is synthetic and its derivation is not validated.
Do not imply medication exposure caused readmission.
Do not send a dashboard without explaining the metrics and their limitations.
portfolio: This is the strongest early portfolio piece: include the original brief, clarification questions, analysis plan, code/workbook, final report and handoff. Show the workflow, not just screenshots.
